title: Rotator Cuff-related Shoulder Pain
case: Case: A 52-year-old electrician has 3 months of right outer shoulder pain, worse overhead and when lying on that side. Passive range is full and painless apart from end range. Painful arc is positive. External rotation strength is pain-limited but strong. Hawkins-Kennedy is positive. Drop arm is negative. No red flags and a normal neck examination.

Working diagnosis: right rotator cuff-related shoulder pain. Plan: education, isometric external rotation and abduction for pain, progression to banded rotation and scaption, thoracic mobility, work-load advice, reassess every 2 to 3 weeks.
plan: education, isometric external rotation and abduction for pain, progression to banded rotation and scaption, thoracic mobility, work-load advice, reassess every 2 to 3 weeks.

differentials.name: Adhesive capsulitis
differentials.key: Marked loss of passive range, especially external rotation

differentials.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
differentials.key: Stiffness, grinding, older age, loss of passive external rotation

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.key: Neck-related arm pain, neurological signs, Spurling positive

differentials.name: AC joint pain
differentials.key: Pain on top of the shoulder, cross-body adduction pain, local tenderness

differentials.name: Biceps-related pain
differentials.key: Anterior shoulder pain, tenderness over the long head

differentials.name: Nerve problem (suprascapular, long thoracic, neuralgic amyotrophy)
differentials.key: Wasting, scapular winging, severe pain then weakness

differentials.name: Referred pain (cardiac, diaphragm, lung apex)
differentials.key: Not changed by shoulder movement, systemic features

qa: Why do we avoid saying the tendon is pinched? Evidence for a pinching mechanism is limited, and the idea may create fear of movement. A load-based explanation is more consistent with the evidence [Ref - to verify].
Why check the neck in a patient with shoulder pain? Neck problems can refer pain to the shoulder, and treating the shoulder alone would not help.
Passive range is greatly reduced in all directions. Which chapter applies? Adhesive capsulitis (Ch 2) or glenohumeral arthritis, not RCRSP.
A 35-year-old cannot lift his arm after a fall. What next? Suspect an acute tear or other injury, protect the shoulder and refer for urgent medical assessment.
Why use isometric exercises first? They can reduce pain without much tendon movement and allow loading when the shoulder is irritable [Ref - to verify].

fields.Purpose: Look for pain in the mid-range of arm elevation, a common feature of RCRSP
fields.Action: Ask the patient to raise the arm out to the side (abduction) and lower it slowly; ask where the pain starts and stops
fields.Positive: Pain in a mid-range arc (often reported between about 60 and 120 degrees), easing at the top or bottom [Ref - to verify]
fields.Supports: A positive result supports a cuff-related source
fields.Limits: Also positive in other shoulder conditions

fields.Purpose: Provoke pain by moving the greater tuberosity toward the area beneath the acromion
fields.Therapist position: Beside the patient; one hand on the elbow and one on the wrist
fields.Action: Raise the arm to 90 degrees of forward flexion with the elbow bent to 90 degrees, then passively rotate the forearm downward (internal rotation)
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar shoulder pain
fields.Supports: Supports a cuff-related pain source when combined with other tests
fields.Limits: Low specificity; many shoulder problems cause pain here [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Moving too fast; allowing trunk rotation; counting a stretch feeling as positive
fields.Next step: Resisted tests for strength and pain

tests.name: Resisted external rotation (infraspinatus) and full/empty can (supraspinatus)

fields.Infraspinatus: Elbow at the side, bent to 90 degrees. Patient pushes the hand outward against the therapist's resistance. Positive: pain or weakness
fields.Supraspinatus (full can): Arm raised in the scapular plane (about 30 degrees forward of the side), thumb pointing up. Patient resists downward pressure. Positive: pain or weakness
fields.Empty can: As above but thumb pointing down. More likely to provoke pain; full can is often preferred [Ref - to verify]
fields.Interpretation: Pain with good strength suggests tendinopathy. Marked weakness suggests a larger tear or a nerve problem

fields.Position and action: Therapist passively lifts the arm to 90 degrees abduction. Patient slowly lowers it
fields.Positive: Arm drops or cannot be lowered smoothly, or severe pain

fields.Position and action: Arm held in about 20 degrees of elevation and near full external rotation. Therapist releases the wrist
fields.Positive: The arm cannot hold the position and drifts inward
fields.Meaning: Suggests a larger supraspinatus or infraspinatus tear

fields.Position and action: Hand behind the back, lift the hand away from the back (lift-off); or press the abdomen with the elbow forward (belly press)
fields.Positive: Cannot lift the hand away, or the elbow drops back

redFlags.Finding: Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness with left shoulder or arm pain
Fall or injury with deformity, inability to move the arm, or severe pain
redFlags.Immediate action: Support the arm; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: Sudden inability to lift the arm after injury or lift, especially under 60 years
redFlags.Urgency: Urgent medical review (early repair may be considered) [Ref - to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Weight loss, cancer history, constant night pain, hard mass
Shoulder and arm pain with Horner signs (droopy eyelid, small pupil), hand muscle wasting, smoker
Arm swelling, pain and colour change
Bilateral shoulder stiffness and aching with morning stiffness, older age, fatigue
redFlags.Immediate action: Refer; ask about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain

manual.name: Thoracic spine mobilization
manual.why: May ease shoulder movement and short-term pain [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: Stiff thoracic spine with raised-arm pain
manual.application: Prone or sitting, gentle central or unilateral glides

manual.name: Glenohumeral mobilization
manual.application: Supine, gentle oscillations in a pain-free range

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education plus an exercise program. Manual therapy is optional for short-term symptom relief. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs a tendon, frees a trapped tendon or fixes scapular position. Evidence supports exercise as the main component [Ref - to verify].
Is it working? Look for easier arm elevation, a smaller painful arc and better overhead or lifting function.

exercise.Objective: Pain relief and early cuff loading
exercise.Steps: Standing sideways, elbow at 90 degrees, push the back of the hand into a wall; hold
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice daily [Ref - to verify]
exercise.Regress when: Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasts into next day

exercise.Steps: Stand beside a wall, arm slightly out, push the elbow into the wall
Elbow at the side with a rolled towel, rotate out against a light band

exercise.Exercise: Side-lying external rotation or prone row

exercise.Steps: Arm raised in the scapular plane with a light weight

exercise.Exercise: Serratus wall slide or push-up plus
exercise.Steps: Hands on wall, slide up and press
Gradual overhead press, carry, throwing progression

exerciseNotes: Principle: exercise loads the tendon at a level the patient tolerates and then increases gradually. Pain during exercise of up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is commonly used as a guide [Ref - to verify]. Do not choose exercises to fix position alone.
Symptom rule: discomfort that settles quickly is acceptable. Pain that stays high into the next day means reduce load. New weakness, numbness or night pain means reassess.

modalities.name: Therapeutic ultrasound
modalities.comment: Weak or no added benefit [Ref - to verify]

modalities.name: Extracorporeal shockwave
modalities.indicated: Possible option mainly in calcific tendinopathy

modalities.name: Taping
modalities.comment: Short-term cue or comfort; no proven healing effect

modalityNotes: Medical options: corticosteroid injection may reduce pain in the short term but may not improve long-term outcomes and has been associated with tendon risks in some studies [Ref - to verify]. Decisions about injections and surgery belong to the doctor. Trials of subacromial decompression surgery have not shown clear benefit over placebo surgery or exercise for many people [Ref - to verify].
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Neck source? Cervical screen positive: go to Vol 2.
Large loss of passive range? Yes: frozen shoulder or arthritis pathway.
Lateral shoulder pain, mid-range painful arc, resisted pain with normal passive range? Yes: working diagnosis is rotator cuff-related shoulder pain.
Drop arm, lag sign or marked weakness, or recent trauma? Yes: suspect a larger tear; refer for imaging.
Visit 1: screen flags and the neck, explain what RCRSP is and that it usually improves with loading, reassure about scan findings, advise on load.
Early: relative rest from the worst aggravators (not complete rest), isometrics, gentle movement.
